newsitem.title: USA: Brady debt falls from heights on weak U.S. bonds.
newsitem.headline: Brady debt falls from heights on weak U.S. bonds.

text.p: Emerging debt market Latin American Brady bonds soared to fresh highs early Tuesday but then sank heavily amid renewed fears of an imminent Federal Reserve rate hike, traders said.

"The levels we hit this morning were pretty impressive, especially in FRBs and C-bonds," said David Heffernan, vice president at Smith Barney. "The Bradies went up on their own and they came down with the bond."
Argentina FRBs reached a year-to-date high of 84-5/8 but closed one point lower at 82-5/8. Brazilian C bonds broke up to 70-1/8 before falling 1-3/8 to 68-1/4.
Brady bonds gave back their gains from the powerful rally as the U.S. Treasury market slipped.

"It was mostly on the T-bond," said Olivier Lemaigre, emerging markets strategist at Citicorp Securities of the Brady afternoon slump. "It was used as an excuse to take profits, but it was also a reminder of the high corelation between our market and short-term U.S. rates,"
The Treasury market fell when comments by a senior Fed official fueled fears of an imminent Fed rate hike. The official said that eight of 12 Fed banks requested a hike in the U.S. discount rate.
The Fed official also said he saw a concensus for a 25 basis point rate hike at the Fed's September 24 meeting.
Brady traders said they would be closely watching the U.S. jobless claims and Philadelphia Fed survey on Thursday for further clues as to Fed policy.
But Brady traders were sanguine about prospects for the emerging markets as spreads against U.S. Treasuries held firm despite the price drops.
"This last gasp up was fueled by short covering," said one Brady trader said. "That kind of extension needed little bit of pullback. We're back to a little more realistic levels."
The recent strength of emerging debt markets was based in strong buying from a broad base of clients, and this interest was likely to persiste, traders said.
"I think they are not trading sorts of buyers, they are buy and hold buyers," Heffernan said. "They are going to come back in when they feel a little more confident about the U.S. bond market."

Rumors that Argentina was contemplating a Mexican-style Brady bond swap cuirculated through the market, but traders seemed skeptical. Given Argentina's heavy debt amortization schedule ahead, analysts suspected the country would not be the most likely candidate for a buy back.
Brady traders said they would be closely watching the progress of tax measures in the Argentine Congress on Wednesday.
